MATH.01.note: Stanford's entry explains the first and second incompleteness theorems, their formal assumptions, and common overstatements about what Gödel proved.

exercise.prompt: Write down the difference between consistency, completeness, and decidability, then explain which property each incompleteness theorem limits.

MATH.02.note: The Stanford entry develops Bayes' theorem from conditional probability and distinguishes the mathematical rule from broader Bayesian inference.

exercise.prompt: Choose a medical-test example with a low base rate and calculate the posterior probability after one positive result.

MATH.03.note: Stanford's set-theory overview introduces cardinality, Cantor's theory of the infinite, and why different infinite sets can have different sizes.

exercise.prompt: Construct a diagonal argument showing that binary sequences cannot be completely listed, then connect it to the uncountability of the real numbers.

MATH.04.note: The Clay Mathematics Institute gives the official Millennium Prize framing of efficient verification, efficient solution, and the significance of P versus NP.

exercise.prompt: Take one search problem such as Sudoku or travelling salesperson and separate the work needed to verify a proposed answer from the work needed to find one.

MATH.05.note: MIT's signals-and-systems lecture treats the Fourier transform as the continuous-frequency extension of Fourier-series analysis.

exercise.prompt: Generate a signal made from two sine waves, plot it in time, compute its discrete Fourier transform, and identify the two frequency peaks.

MATH.06.note: MathWorld gives a compact derivation and reference treatment of Euler's formula, from which Euler's identity follows by substituting pi.

exercise.prompt: Use the power-series expansions of exponential, sine, and cosine to derive Euler's formula term by term.

MATH.07.note: Scholarpedia's expert-authored history connects nonlinear dynamical systems, sensitive dependence, attractors, bifurcations, and deterministic chaos.

exercise.prompt: Iterate the logistic map for two initial values that differ only in the sixth decimal place and graph how their trajectories separate.

MATH.08.note: MIT's plane-geometry and topology course supplies an accessible route into continuity, deformation, winding, and topological invariants.

article.title: Geometry and Topology in the Plane

exercise.prompt: Classify several drawn shapes by connected components and holes, then explain which can be continuously deformed into one another.

MATH.09.note: NIST's Monte Carlo tool and documentation provide a practical institutional introduction to simulation-based uncertainty analysis.

article.title: Monte Carlo Tool
article.source: National Institute of Standards and Technology

exercise.prompt: Estimate pi by sampling random points in a square, counting those inside the inscribed circle, and plotting error against sample size.

MATH.10.note: NIST's normal-distribution handbook entry explains the distribution and explicitly identifies the central limit theorem as its main theoretical justification.

exercise.prompt: Simulate repeated samples from a strongly skewed distribution and compare histograms of the raw values with histograms of their sample means.

MATH.11.note: MIT's opening graph-theory lecture introduces graphs as mathematical objects and connects structural questions to modern combinatorics.

article.title: Lecture 1: Introduction to Graph Theory and Additive Combinatorics

exercise.prompt: Model the Seven Bridges of Königsberg as a graph, calculate every vertex degree, and use Euler's criterion to explain why the walk is impossible.

MATH.12.note: Princeton's programming assignment turns the birthday collision result into an experiment and connects probability calculations with simulation.

exercise.prompt: Simulate rooms of increasing size until the shared-birthday probability crosses 50 percent, then compare the simulation with the exact formula.
